name: Finance: Out-of-sample portfolio choice against 1/N (20 size and value portfolios and the market)
description: Choose each month's portfolio of 20 size and book-to-market portfolios and the market using only the previous 120 months of returns. The evaluator recomputes the Sharpe ratio of the next-month returns net of 50 bp trading costs over 1973-07 to 2025-09 and compares it with the 1/N rule.

sources.locator: Sections 2-3 and Tables 2-5: dataset 5 (FF-1-factor: 20 size/book-to-market portfolios and the market, N = 21), 120-month rolling windows, relative weights, Sharpe ratio and 50 bp costs.

25 portfolios formed on size and book-to-market (value-weighted; the five largest-size portfolios are dropped as in DGU) and Fama/French market and T-bill series, monthly; CRSP 202509 files pinned in catalog/finance-data-lock.json.

requirements.datasets: Kenneth R. French Data Library monthly tables (ff25_vw_monthly.csv, ff_factors_monthly.csv; CRSP 202509 vintage) fetched by scripts/prepare_finance.py from pinned Internet Archive snapshots and verified by SHA-256; not redistributed.

evaluation.benchmark: Finance: Out-of-sample portfolio choice against 1/N (20 size and value portfolios and the market)
evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: choose_weights(excess_returns, context) -> array of N finite positions x. excess_returns is a (120, N) float array of the previous 120 monthly excess returns (decimal, oldest first) of the task's N assets; context = {'cost_rate': 0.005, 'window': 120, 'max_gross': 20.0, 'risk_free': (120,) monthly T-bill returns, 'previous_weights': drifted relative weights just before rebalancing (None in the first month)}. The evaluator forms DeMiguel-Garlappi-Uppal relative weights w = x/|sum(x)| (sum(x) must be nonzero and sum|w| <= 20), holds w for the next month, charges 0.5% of sum|w - previous_weights| per rebalance and requires wealth to stay positive. Score: monthly Sharpe ratio of the net out-of-sample excess returns over every month of the task period (maximize); the 1/N rule is recomputed on the same months for comparison

limitations: The evaluation months are public and fixed. Strategies or hyperparameters tuned on them overfit, and a candidate that reads the prepared files or embeds remembered returns could look ahead; the evaluator only prevents look-ahead through its interface. Treat scores as development scores and freeze a candidate before testing it on months after 2025-09.

A monthly Sharpe ratio estimated from 50 to 52 years of returns has a standard error of about 0.04, so differences from 1/N below that size are not statistically meaningful; the one-sided Jobson-Korkie-Memmel p-value against 1/N is reported in the details.

Returns are value-weighted CRSP portfolio returns from the CRSP 202509 vintage of the French library; later vintages revise history slightly. Costs are a flat 50 bp of traded value with no market impact, borrowing spread, short-sale fees or taxes, and positions are financed at the one-month T-bill rate.

Deviations from DeMiguel, Garlappi and Uppal: the scored period extends to 2025-09, returns are net of costs (their Sharpe table is gross), the first allocation is free, gross exposure is capped at 20 and a strategy whose wealth reaches zero is invalid.

state_of_the_art.statement: No published value exists for this exact protocol. On DGU's 1963-07 to 2004-11 sample, 1/N has a monthly Sharpe ratio of 0.1623 for this dataset and the constrained minimum-variance rule 0.1546; the local 1/N seed scores 0.1501 net of costs over 1973-07 to 2025-09.

sources.title: Optimal Versus Naive Diversification: How Inefficient is the 1/N Portfolio Strategy?

science_relevance.scientific_problem: Choose portfolio weights that perform well out of sample when expected returns and covariances must be estimated from short return histories.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Estimation error can make optimized portfolios worse than naive diversification; DGU find that none of 14 optimizing models reliably beats 1/N, so robust portfolio choice remains a central problem for investors and for asset-pricing research.

papers.title: Optimal Versus Naive Diversification: How Inefficient is the 1/N Portfolio Strategy?
papers.primary_goal: Determine whether portfolio rules derived from mean-variance optimization, including rules designed to reduce estimation error, outperform naive 1/N diversification out of sample.
papers.task_relation: The local task applies DGU's rolling-window protocol to their dataset 5 (20 size/book-to-market portfolios and the market) on a longer sample and scores net-of-cost Sharpe ratios.

science_relevance.reason: The cited paper's main objective is the out-of-sample performance of portfolio rules relative to 1/N, which is exactly what the task scores.
